data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: Japan spent most of the period fighting deflation: inflation was 0.3% in 2006, negative in 2009-11, and near zero through the 2010s despite the Bank of Japan's 2013 quantitative and qualitative easing and yield-curve control. The 2014 consumption-tax hike briefly lifted it to 2.8%. The global 2022 shock finally broke the deflationary mindset, with inflation reaching 2.5% in 2022, 3.3% in 2023, and a projected 3.2% in 2025, and the BOJ ended negative rates in March 2024. After decades of undershooting, Japan now faces the novel challenge of keeping inflation from overshooting while normalizing policy.
debt_management: Japan has the developed world's highest public debt: 152.1% of GDP in 2006, rising through the GFC (172.9% in 2009), the 2011 earthquake, and Abenomics-era stimulus to 206.3% in 2019, then 228.8% in 2020 on COVID, easing to a projected 206.5% in 2025. It has remained sustainable because it is overwhelmingly domestically held, the BOJ owns roughly half, and borrowing costs stayed near zero for years. In dollar terms GDP fell from $5.3tn (2012) to a projected $4.4tn (2025) on yen weakness, flattering the ratio. The risk is rising interest costs as rates normalize.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis hit exports hard; debt jumped past 170% of GDP.
Tohoku earthquake, tsunami, and Fukushima disaster; massive reconstruction spending followed.
Abenomics launched; BOJ began QQE in April 2013 targeting 2% inflation.
Consumption tax raised to 10%, denting demand just before COVID.
COVID-19; debt hit 228.8% of GDP on emergency spending.
Yen slid sharply; BOJ defended yield-curve control amid global tightening.
BOJ ended negative rates and YCC, beginning cautious normalization.

outlook_next_decade: Japan's base case is low but positive growth with inflation settling near 2% and very gradual policy normalization. The debt trajectory depends on interest rates: sustained higher yields would eventually raise debt-service costs materially, though domestic ownership provides a deep buffer. Demographics remain the structural drag, partially offset by productivity gains and corporate reform. The analytical risk is a disorderly bond-market repricing if fiscal discipline slips; the upside is that escaping deflation durably would be a historic success.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
